A plain tokio::spawn is not waited for and ends with its thread; work that must outlive the subscription goes through MainRuntime::spawn. The threads pay from about ten microseconds of computation per delivery; on lighter handlers they cost more CPU than they save. Diagnostics find the handlers that need them. Under TestApp the threads run as n workers on the test's runtime.

Macros Manual examples/threads.rs /// Runs on one of the subscription's eight threads, from the first poll to the end; the app's /// runtime stays free for I/O and for the other subscriptions. #[subscriber("images.resize", threads(8), reply)] async fn resize(job: &Resize, Ctx(main): Ctx<MainRuntime>) -> Resized { let checksum = render(job); // The explicit way back to the app's runtime; what it sends must be `Send`. main.spawn(notify(job.id)); Resized { id: job.id, checksum, } } examples/manual/threads.rs /// Runs on one of the subscription's eight threads, from the first poll to the end; the app's /// runtime stays free for I/O and for the other subscriptions. struct ResizeImage; impl Handle<Resize, Resized> for ResizeImage { fn handle( &self, job: &Resize, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Resized, HandlerOutcome>> { let checksum = render(job); // The explicit way back to the app's runtime; what it sends must be `Send`. ctx.main_runtime().spawn(notify(job.id)); ready(Ok(Resized { id: job.id, checksum, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("images", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("images.resize", ResizeImage) .threads(nonzero!(8)) .reply() .build(), ) }) }

The dedicated threads and the app runtime's threads share the machine's cores, and Tokio starts one worker per core by default. A service with threads(n) sizes the app's runtime for its I/O. #[ruststream::app] takes the runtime arguments of #[tokio::main]: flavor = "current_thread" or worker_threads = n. A current-thread runtime beside dedicated threads gives the rest of the service the lowest latency. In the manual form, main passes an AppRuntime to run_main_on. Macros Manual examples/threads.rs /// The dedicated threads carry the computation, so the app's runtime needs one thread for I/O. #[ruststream::app(flavor = "current_thread")] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("images", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(resize)) } examples/manual/threads.rs /// What `#[ruststream::app(flavor = "current_thread")]` writes: the dedicated threads carry the /// computation, so the app's runtime needs one thread for I/O. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main_on(AppRuntime::CurrentThread, app) }

workers(n) handles up to n deliveries of one subscription at once; workers(n, by_key) keeps the deliveries of one key in order. The subscription starts n long-lived workers, tasks of the runtime the app runs on. A free worker takes the next delivery. While n deliveries are in flight, the subscription does not read the broker, so back-pressure holds. Deliveries finish in any order: the subscription's global order is lost. Workers suit a handler that waits on I/O; a handler that computes belongs on threads. The setting is a clause of the attribute, or .workers(n) among the mount-site settings. The count is a NonZeroUsize, and nonzero! writes one. A router chain takes a Workers value through Router::workers. Handing a delivery to a worker allocates nothing. A batch handler gets a pool of batches, each batch in a task of its own. On shutdown, the deliveries in flight finish within the app's shutdown_timeout.

Four charges that each wait a second on a payment provider take one second together. Macros Manual examples/workers.rs /// Up to four orders are charged at once; the next one waits for a free worker. #[subscriber("orders", workers(4))] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { charge(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/workers.rs /// Up to four orders are charged at once; the next one waits for a free worker. fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Bill).workers(nonzero!(4)).build()) }) }

workers(n, by_key) makes the same n workers into n sequential lanes. A delivery goes to the lane picked by hashing its partition key, which the broker's message reports through Partitioned. Deliveries with one key never reorder, and deliveries with different keys run at once. A delivery without a key rotates over the lanes. The in-memory broker reads the key from the partition-key header. At the mount site the setting is .workers_by_key(n). Macros Manual examples/workers.rs /// Four lanes by the message's partition key: one customer's orders are charged in order, /// different customers' at once. #[subscriber("orders", workers(4, by_key))] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { charge(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/workers.rs /// Four lanes by the message's partition key: one customer's orders are charged in order, /// different customers' at once. fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Bill) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)) .build(), ) }) }

What a subscriber does when its handler panics or a payload cannot decode, set per subscriber with on_failure. A subscriber carries two policies: one for a handler panic, one for a delivery that cannot decode. A panic fails fast by default, and a test reads it with panicked: a loud error names the subscription, the service shuts down gracefully, and run returns an error, so an orchestrator restarts it. Fail fast takes effect under an unwinding panic profile; with panic = "abort" the process is already gone. A decode failure drops the delivery by default: one malformed payload does not stop the consumer, and assert_last_failed_to_decode checks it in a test. A decode failure is a payload the codec rejects, a header contract that does not parse, a missing carried value, or a delivery the broker reports unreadable. Each policy is a FailurePolicy: fail_fast, drop, retry, retry_after(delay) or skip. drop, retry and retry_after(delay) settle the way the handler outcomes of the same name do. skip acks the delivery to move past it; the message is gone and was never handled. retry and retry_after bring the delivery back, so a payload that never decodes keeps coming back. The attribute takes on_failure(panic = .., decode = ..), with either key alone; the manual form takes a FailurePolicies value.

Macros Manual examples/failure_policy.rs /// No clause: a payload that cannot decode is dropped, and a panic stops the service. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn fulfil(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { assert_ne!(order.id, 0, "an order without an id reached fulfilment"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/failure_policy.rs /// No settings step: a payload that cannot decode is dropped, and a panic stops the service. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<Order> for Fulfil { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { assert_ne!(order.id, 0, "an order without an id reached fulfilment"); ready(Ok(())) } }

Macros Manual examples/failure_policy.rs /// An audit trail moves past anything it cannot process: both failures ack the delivery. #[subscriber("orders", on_failure(panic = skip, decode = skip))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { assert_ne!(order.id, 0, "an order without an id reached the audit"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/failure_policy.rs /// An audit trail moves past anything it cannot process: both failures ack the delivery. struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { assert_ne!(order.id, 0, "an order without an id reached the audit"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Audit) .on_failure( FailurePolicies::default() .with_panic(FailurePolicy::Skip) .with_decode(FailurePolicy::Skip), ) .build(), ) }) }

A panic still stops the service. #[subscriber("orders", on_failure(decode = retry_after(SCHEMA_ROLLOUT)))] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/failure_policy.rs const SCHEMA_ROLLOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); /// Producers roll a schema change out first: a payload this version cannot read yet comes /// back in a minute instead of being dropped. An enum deriving InMessages declares several message types on one subscription: a rule picks the variant, and the document lists one message per variant. The set is an enum whose variants each wrap one model, and the handler takes a reference to the enum: &OrderEvent, or &[OrderEvent] for a batch. Each model derives MessageInfo, because the document lists it by that name. A model decodes through its own path: the codec of the mount for a serde type, its own reader for a type that derives Deserialized, such as a Protobuf message. One set may hold both, so a JSON event and a Protobuf event share a subscription and each shows its own format in the document. The derive is the receiving counterpart of OutMessages, which declares what a slot sends. The header rule is the one to reach for when the producer can set a header. #[in_messages(header = "event")] on the enum names the header the set reads, and #[in_messages(value = "..")] on each variant names the value that picks it. The chosen variant decodes once; a set costs what a single type costs, plus the header lookup. A delivery without the header, or with a value no variant declares, is a decode failure naming the header and the value seen, settled by the failure policy like any other. The document carries the rule: each message's headers schema lists the header with its const value. A rule of your own is a function: #[in_messages(discriminate = path)] names one that reads the delivery, its headers and raw payload, and returns which kind to decode. The derive generates the kind enum, OrderUpdateKind for a set OrderUpdate, with one unit variant per model. The function returning None is a decode failure naming the set. This is the form for a rule no attribute states: a schema id, a field of the payload, a shape of the bytes. A broker crate may ship such a function for its own format. A rule only the decode codec can answer is a type: #[in_messages(discriminate_with_codec = ByRecord)] names one that implements CodecDiscriminator. A schema registry is the case: each record carries a schema id, and only the registry codec knows which record the id stands for. The type's kind(codec, msg) reads the codec of the scope or router and the delivery, and returns the kind the way a function does; None is the same decode failure. An impl that bounds the codec makes the set mount only under codecs that satisfy the bound: a set mounted under a codec that cannot answer is a compile error at the mount site. The call is static, so a delivery pays only for what the type itself does. Such a set decodes per codec, so it does not implement InMessages itself: it is a handler input everywhere a set is, and a bound of your own written as T: InMessages does not accept it. A broker crate may ship the type for its own registry. A set with no rule tries its variants left to right, and the first that decodes wins. The order of the variants is the rule, so put the strictest model first. Every variant failing is one decode failure that carries each variant's error. Each attempt costs one decode of that variant, so a delivery of the last variant pays for every variant before it. Left to right is exact only as far as the formats are strict: a Protobuf reader skips the fields it does not know, so a payload of one Protobuf model may decode as another, and a JSON object with the right fields decodes as any model that has them. For such sets, name a rule, or order the variants from the strictest to the loosest. The derive checks the declaration: every variant wraps exactly one model, each model implements MessageInfo, a model appears once in a set, the enum takes no generic parameters, and a variant owns its model, so a type that borrows the payload cannot be one. A set is not a message, so MessageInfo is not derived on the set itself. Each of these is a compile error on the variant or the enum it concerns. A serde enum with #[serde(tag = "..")] or #[serde(untagged)] is still an ordinary input type, but it is not a set: it works for serde formats only, the tagged form buffers the whole payload per delivery, the untagged form needs a self-describing format, and the document shows one message for the enum.

The header rule, on a set of a JSON model and a Protobuf one: Macros Manual examples/in_messages.rs /// Every event of an order on the `orders` subscription: the `event` header names the model. #[derive(InMessages)] #[in_messages(header = "event")] enum OrderEvent { #[in_messages(value = "created")] Created(OrderCreated), #[in_messages(value = "cancelled")] Cancelled(OrderCancelled), } examples/manual/in_messages.rs /// Every event of an order on the `orders` subscription: the `event` header names the model. enum OrderEvent { Created(OrderCreated), Cancelled(OrderCancelled), } /// The kinds of the set, what a discriminator names; the derive generates this enum. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)] enum OrderEventKind { Created, Cancelled, } impl InMessages for OrderEvent { type Kind = OrderEventKind; fn decode<DecodeCodec, M>(codec: &DecodeCodec, msg: &M) -> Result<Self, CodecError> where DecodeCodec: Codec, M: IncomingMessage, { let kind = match msg.headers().get("event") { Some(b"created") => OrderEventKind::Created, Some(b"cancelled") => OrderEventKind::Cancelled, Some(other) => { return Err(CodecError::Decode( format!( "the `event` header is `{}`, which names no variant of `OrderEvent`", String::from_utf8_lossy(other) ) .into(), )); } None => { return Err(CodecError::Decode( "the delivery carries no `event` header".into(), )); } }; // The chosen variant decodes once, through its model's own path. let payload = msg.payload(); match kind { OrderEventKind::Created => { <OrderCreated as InVariant<Self>>::decode_variant(codec, payload) .map(OrderEvent::Created) } OrderEventKind::Cancelled => { <OrderCancelled as InVariant<Self>>::decode_variant(codec, payload) .map(OrderEvent::Cancelled) } } } // One entry per model, in the order of the variants, each with the header value that names // it; the document lists them as the messages of the subscription. fn incoming() -> Vec<IncomingMessageMetadata> { vec![ <OrderCreated as InVariant<Self>>::describe() .with_discriminator(HeaderDiscriminator::new("event", "created")), <OrderCancelled as InVariant<Self>>::describe() .with_discriminator(HeaderDiscriminator::new("event", "cancelled")), ] } } impl Input for OrderEvent { type Axis = SoloSet<Self>; } The handler matches on the set. The function reads the delivery and names the kind to decode. #[derive(InMessages)] #[in_messages(discriminate = by_payload_shape)] enum OrderUpdate { Created(OrderCreated), Cancelled(OrderCancelled), } fn by_payload_shape(message: &impl IncomingMessage) -> Option<OrderUpdateKind> { match message.payload().first()? { b'{' => Some(OrderUpdateKind::Created), _ => Some(OrderUpdateKind::Cancelled), } } #[subscriber("orders.updates")] async fn on_update(update: &OrderUpdate) -> HandlerOutcome { match update { OrderUpdate::Created(created) => tracing::info!(created.id, "created"), OrderUpdate::Cancelled(cancelled) => tracing::info!(cancelled.id, "cancelled"), } HandlerOutcome::ack() } A rule that asks the decode codec: the codec names records, and the set mounts under it through a router. examples/in_messages.rs /// What a registry codec answers beside decoding: the record a schema id stands for. trait RecordNames: Codec { fn record_name(&self, schema: &[u8]) -> Option<&'static str>; } /// JSON whose records a schema registry names; the registry here is a fixed table. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)] struct Registry; impl Codec for Registry { fn encode<T: Serialize>(&self, value: &T) -> Result<BytesMut, CodecError> { JsonCodec.encode(value) } fn decode<T: DeserializeOwned>(&self, bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<T, CodecError> { JsonCodec.decode(bytes) } } impl RecordNames for Registry { fn record_name(&self, schema: &[u8]) -> Option<&'static str> { match schema { b"1" => Some("OrderCreated"), b"2" => Some("OrderPlaced"), _ => None, } } } /// An order was placed through the legacy checkout: the same JSON shape as `OrderCreated`, so /// only the registry tells the two apart. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema, MessageInfo)] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, } /// Records named by the registry the scope codec holds: every delivery carries a schema id, /// and only the codec knows which record it stands for. #[derive(InMessages)] #[in_messages(discriminate_with_codec = ByRecord)] enum OrderRecord { Created(OrderCreated), Placed(OrderPlaced), } /// Asks the codec which record the `schema` header names. It accepts every codec that names /// records, so the set mounts only under such a codec. struct ByRecord; impl<DecodeCodec: RecordNames> CodecDiscriminator<OrderRecordKind, DecodeCodec> for ByRecord { fn kind<M: IncomingMessage>(codec: &DecodeCodec, msg: &M) -> Option<OrderRecordKind> { match codec.record_name(msg.headers().get("schema")?)? { "OrderCreated" => Some(OrderRecordKind::Created), "OrderPlaced" => Some(OrderRecordKind::Placed), _ => None, } } } #[subscriber("orders.records")] async fn on_record(record: &OrderRecord) -> HandlerOutcome { match record { OrderRecord::Created(created) => tracing::info!(created.id, "created"), OrderRecord::Placed(placed) => tracing::info!(placed.id, "placed"), } HandlerOutcome::ack() } Left to right, the strictest model first: examples/in_messages.rs /// No rule: the variants are tried in their order, and the first that decodes wins. The JSON /// model comes first because it is the stricter one: a Protobuf reader skips what it does not /// know, so Protobuf bytes never pass as JSON while the reverse could happen. #[derive(InMessages)] enum OrderChange { Created(OrderCreated), Cancelled(OrderCancelled), } #[subscriber("orders.changes")] async fn on_change(change: &OrderChange) -> HandlerOutcome { match change { OrderChange::Created(created) => tracing::info!(created.id, "created"), OrderChange::Cancelled(cancelled) => tracing::info!(cancelled.id, "cancelled"), } HandlerOutcome::ack() }
What a handler returns settles its delivery: ack, retry, retry after a delay, or drop, as a HandlerOutcome.

and_after attaches a continuation to an outcome: work that runs on a task of its own once the delivery is settled. HandlerOutcome::ack().and_after(fut) settles the delivery first, then runs fut. A continuation attaches to any of the outcomes, drop() and retry() included; a second and_after replaces the first. On a batch each element carries its own continuation, so only the elements that asked for one run it. Post-settle work is at most once: the delivery is already settled, so a lost or panicking continuation never brings it back. Work whose loss must redeliver the message belongs in the body, before the settlement. A graceful shutdown waits for running continuations within the app's shutdown_timeout. A test waits for them with drain. A hook on the context runs after the settlement too, gated by which settlement it was.

HandlerOutcome::ack() .and_after(async move { notifier.send(format!("accepted {id}")).await }) } examples/manual/post_settle.rs /// The outcome with its continuation travels as `Err(outcome)`: a plain `Ok(())` acks with /// none. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), Arc<Notifier>> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Notifier>>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let notifier = Arc::clone(ctx.state()); let id = order.id; // Runs once the ack is through; losing it never brings the order back. ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::ack().and_after(async move { notifier.send(format!("accepted {id}")).await; }))) } }

What the handler body returns settles the delivery: a HandlerOutcome, nothing at all, or a Result. HandlerOutcome::ack() acknowledges the delivery, and the broker forgets it. HandlerOutcome::retry() asks for it again at once; on the in-memory broker it returns to the same subscriber. HandlerOutcome::drop() rejects it without a redelivery; a broker with a dead-letter policy of its own applies it. HandlerOutcome::retry_after(delay) is the fourth settlement, described on the retry_after page. A body that returns () acks every delivery. A body that returns Result<(), E> acks on Ok and drops on Err; the error value is discarded, so log it in the body when it matters. A body that returns Result<HandlerOutcome, E> settles by the inner outcome on Ok and drops on Err. A batch body answers the same way, with one HandlerOutcome for the whole slice or a Vec<HandlerOutcome> with one per element. A manual body always returns Result<(), HandlerOutcome>: Ok(()) acks, and Err(outcome) settles by that outcome. A retry() with no cap declared comes back for as long as the body keeps asking; the attempt cap ends that. Any outcome can carry work for after the settlement with and_after. A panic or a payload that does not decode is settled by the failure policy instead. A test reads the settlements with outcomes.

Macros Manual examples/handler_outcome.rs /// Stands in for a stock service whose first reservation finds the shelf locked. struct Warehouse { locked: AtomicBool, } impl Warehouse { fn try_reserve(&self, _sku: &str) -> bool { !self.locked.swap(false, Ordering::SeqCst) } } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn reserve(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Warehouse>>) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.sku.is_empty() { // Nothing to reserve, and a redelivery would not change that. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if !ctx.state().try_reserve(&order.sku) { // A passing condition: the broker brings the order back. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/handler_outcome.rs /// Stands in for a stock service whose first reservation finds the shelf locked. struct Warehouse { locked: AtomicBool, } impl Warehouse { fn try_reserve(&self, _sku: &str) -> bool { !self.locked.swap(false, Ordering::SeqCst) } } struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), Arc<Warehouse>> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Warehouse>>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.sku.is_empty() { // Nothing to reserve, and a redelivery would not change that. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } if !ctx.state().try_reserve(&order.sku) { // A passing condition: the broker brings the order back. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } ready(Ok(())) } }

A post-settle hook registered on the context runs once the delivery is settled, only for the settlement it names. ctx.after_ack(fut) registers a hook that runs only when the delivery is acked. ctx.after(outcome) returns an After, and its then(fut) runs only when the settlement matches that outcome by kind; retry_after matches any delay. ctx.after_settle(fut) runs whatever the settlement. Hooks accumulate, and every matching one runs. On a batch the context belongs to the whole batch: only after_settle hooks run there, once, after every element is settled. A hook is at most once, like a continuation of and_after: a lost or panicking hook never brings the delivery back. A graceful shutdown waits for running hooks within the app's shutdown_timeout, and a test waits for them with drain.

Macros Manual examples/post_settle.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Notifier>>) -> HandlerOutcome { let id = order.id; let notifier = Arc::clone(ctx.state()); ctx.after_ack(async move { notifier.send(format!("shipping {id}")).await }); let notifier = Arc::clone(ctx.state()); ctx.after(HandlerOutcome::drop()) .then(async move { notifier.send(format!("rejected {id}")).await }); let notifier = Arc::clone(ctx.state()); ctx.after_settle(async move { notifier.send(format!("settled {id}")).await }); if id == 0 { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/post_settle.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), Arc<Notifier>> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Notifier>>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let id = order.id; let notifier = Arc::clone(ctx.state()); ctx.after_ack(async move { notifier.send(format!("shipping {id}")).await }); let notifier = Arc::clone(ctx.state()); ctx.after(HandlerOutcome::drop()) .then(async move { notifier.send(format!("rejected {id}")).await }); let notifier = Arc::clone(ctx.state()); ctx.after_settle(async move { notifier.send(format!("settled {id}")).await }); if id == 0 { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } ready(Ok(())) } }

retry_after(delay) asks for the delivery back no sooner than the delay, for a condition that will pass. It is one of the outcomes, next to an immediate retry(). A broker with native delayed redelivery holds the delivery and returns it after the delay. The in-memory broker is one: the delivery comes back to the same subscriber, and nothing is published. On a broker without it, the runtime drops the delivery and publishes a copy back to the subscription after the delay, through the Retry slot. That copy carries the RETRY_COUNT_HEADER (x-ruststream-retry-count), incremented on every copy. The copy is at most once over the delay: a process that exits before the timer fires loses it. A graceful shutdown waits for pending copies within the app's shutdown_timeout. A zero delay redelivers at once, as retry() does; write retry() when no delay is meant. A batch body sets a delay per element, and only those elements come back. A test runs on a paused clock (#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]), and tb.advance(delay) brings the delivery back, as the advance page shows. How many times a delivery may come back is the registration's declaration, max_attempts.

Macros Manual examples/retry.rs const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(5); #[subscriber("payments")] async fn reconcile( payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Ledger>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if !ctx.state().is_cleared(payment.id) { // The bank has not cleared it yet: an immediate redelivery would only spin. return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "reconciled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/retry.rs const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(5); struct Reconcile; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), (), Arc<Ledger>> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Ledger>>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !ctx.state().is_cleared(payment.id) { // The bank has not cleared it yet: an immediate redelivery would only spin. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "reconciled"); ready(Ok(())) } }

Macros Manual examples/retry.rs const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); /// One outcome per element: a cleared payment is acked, a pending one alone comes back. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn reconcile( payments: &[Payment], ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Ledger>>, ) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if ctx.state().is_cleared(payment.id) { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect() } examples/manual/retry.rs const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); /// One outcome per element: a cleared payment is acked, a pending one alone comes back. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Payment], (), (), (), Arc<Ledger>> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Arc<Ledger>>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Err(payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if ctx.state().is_cleared(payment.id) { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect())) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App<State = Arc<Ledger>> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Arc::new(Ledger::default()))) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("payments", Reconcile) .batch(nonzero!(2)) .start_at(MemoryPosition::start()) .build(), ) }) }

Layers wrap handlers and publishes: app-wide, per router or per registration. A layer wraps a handler: it runs code of its own around each delivery, with the delivery's context. A publish layer wraps a publish: it runs around each message a handler sends. Both are static: the chain is one type built when the code compiles, and a layer costs only its own code. A chain chosen when the app starts, from configuration, goes into a dynamic stack, which boxes each step.

A DynStack is a handler middleware chain assembled when the app starts, mounted on one registration as one layer. A static layer chain is fixed when the code compiles. A DynStack holds a list chosen when the app is built: from configuration, a loop or a feature flag. Each element implements DynMiddleware. It gets the input, the context and a Next; next.run(input, ctx) runs the rest of the chain and the handler. It may return an outcome without that call. DynStack::new(list) freezes the list, and the first element runs outermost. An empty list leaves the handler's behaviour as it is. The stack is one ordinary Layer, fixed to one input type, so it wraps one registration: .layer(stack) right after an include on a router. The app and a router take only layers that wrap any input, which a stack fixed to one type is not. A registration's layer runs outside its decode step, so a stack over the broker's message type, MemoryMessage here, sees the raw delivery. Each element costs one boxed future and one dynamic call per delivery, and the stack one more of each for the handler it wraps; the static layers around it stay free. The middleware has no macro form: the same impl serves both forms, and only the mounting differs.

The middleware drops the deliveries of one tenant. examples/dyn_stack.rs /// Drops the deliveries of one tenant. struct Block { tenant: String, } impl<I: Send + Sync> DynMiddleware<I> for Block { fn handle<'a>( &'a self, input: &'a I, ctx: &'a mut Context<'_>, next: Next<'a, I>, ) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = HandlerOutcome> + Send + 'a>> { Box::pin(async move { if ctx.headers().get("tenant") == Some(self.tenant.as_bytes()) { tracing::warn!(subscription = ctx.name(), tenant = %self.tenant, "blocked"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } next.run(input, ctx).await }) } } The app builds one per tenant the configuration blocks. Macros Manual examples/dyn_stack.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The chain comes from configuration: one `Block` per tenant the operator listed. fn app(blocked: &[&str]) -> impl App { let chain = blocked .iter() .map(|tenant| -> Arc<dyn DynMiddleware<MemoryMessage>> { Arc::new(Block { tenant: (*tenant).to_owned(), }) }); let stack = DynStack::new(chain); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The stack wraps one registration, which sees the broker's own message. b.include_router(Router::new().include(accept).layer(stack)) }) } examples/manual/dyn_stack.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The chain comes from configuration: one `Block` per tenant the operator listed. fn app(blocked: &[&str]) -> impl App { let chain = blocked .iter() .map(|tenant| -> Arc<dyn DynMiddleware<MemoryMessage>> { Arc::new(Block { tenant: (*tenant).to_owned(), }) }); let stack = DynStack::new(chain); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The stack wraps one registration, which sees the broker's own message. b.include_router( Router::new() .include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) .layer(stack), ) }) }

A layer wraps handlers in code of your own: every handler of the app, every handler of a router, or one registration. A Layer<H> turns a handler H into a wrapper of its own type, and that type implements Handler. The wrapper gets the input and the same &mut Context the handler gets, and calls the handler it wraps. It runs code before and after the call, and may return an outcome without making it. Three scopes take a layer. RustStream::layer, before with_broker, wraps every handler the app mounts, router handlers included. Router::layer, before the router's first include, wraps every handler of that router. .layer(..) right after an include on a router wraps that registration alone, outside its decode step. The app and a router hide their handlers' concrete types, so a layer for those scopes also implements BlanketLayer; a registration keeps its type, and Layer<H> is enough there. The app's layers wrap outside a router's. In the app and in a router, the first layer added runs outermost; on a registration, the last one added does. The chain is one type, so a layer adds nothing to the hot path beyond its own code. App and router layers wrap single-message handlers; batch handlers are not wrapped. A layer has no macro form: the same impl serves both forms, and only the mounting differs. A chain chosen when the app starts goes into a DynStack.

The layer drops a delivery that names no tenant before the handler sees it. examples/layer.rs /// Drops a delivery that names no tenant before the handler sees it. #[derive(Clone)] struct RequireTenant; /// The handler `RequireTenant` makes of the one it wraps. struct Tenanted<H>(H); impl<H> Layer<H> for RequireTenant { type Handler = Tenanted<H>; fn layer(&self, inner: H) -> Tenanted<H> { Tenanted(inner) } } impl<M, C, S, H> Handler<M, C, S> for Tenanted<H> where M: Send + Sync, C: Send, S: Send + Sync, H: Handler<M, C, S>, { async fn handle(&self, msg: &M, ctx: &mut Context<'_, C, S>) -> HandlerOutcome { if ctx.headers().get("tenant").is_none() { tracing::warn!(subscription = ctx.name(), "no tenant header, dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } self.0.handle(msg, ctx).await } } // The app and a router wrap handlers whose types they hide, through this generic method. impl BlanketLayer for RequireTenant { fn apply<M, C, S, H>(&self, handler: H) -> impl Handler<M, C, S> + 'static where M: Send + Sync + 'static, C: Send + 'static, S: Send + Sync + 'static, H: Handler<M, C, S> + 'static, { Tenanted(handler) } } Mounted on the app, it wraps every handler. Macros Manual examples/layer.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Every handler the app mounts below runs inside the layer. .layer(RequireTenant) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept)) } examples/manual/layer.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Every handler the app mounts below runs inside the layer. .layer(RequireTenant) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Log).build()) }) }

On a fresh router the layer wraps every handler of the router. After an include it wraps that registration alone. Macros Manual examples/layer.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // Before the first `include`: every handler of this router. b.include_router(Router::new().layer(RequireTenant).include(refund)) // After an `include`: that registration alone; `audit` runs unwrapped. .include_router( Router::new() .include(invoice) .layer(RequireTenant) .include(audit), ) }) } examples/manual/layer.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // Before the first `include`: every handler of this router. b.include_router( Router::new() .layer(RequireTenant) .include(subscriber("refunds", Log).build()), ) // After an `include`: that registration alone; `audit` runs unwrapped. .include_router( Router::new() .include(subscriber("invoices", Log).build()) .layer(RequireTenant) .include(subscriber("audit", Log).build()), ) }) }

A PublishDynStack is a publish middleware chain assembled when the app starts, added to the app as one publish layer. A PublishDynStack holds a list chosen when the app is built: from configuration, a loop or a feature flag. Each element implements PublishDynLayer. It gets the outgoing message and a PublishDynNext; next.run(out) runs the rest of the list and then the static chain around the stack. PublishDynStack::new(list) freezes the list, and the first element runs outermost. The stack is a PublishLayer itself, added with RustStream::publish_layer, so it wraps the same publishes as any other. Each element costs one boxed future and one dynamic call per publish, and the stack two boxes more: its continuation and the future of the chain after it. The static layers around it stay free. The layer has no macro form: the same impl serves both forms, and only the handler differs.

The layer writes one header on every message. examples/publish_dyn_stack.rs /// Writes one header on every message the app publishes. struct Stamp { // Both clone by reference count, so a publish copies no bytes. name: Str, value: Bytes, } impl PublishDynLayer for Stamp { fn on_publish<'a>( &'a self, out: &'a mut Outgoing<'a>, next: PublishDynNext<'a>, ) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>>> + Send + 'a>> { out.headers_mut() .insert(self.name.clone(), self.value.clone()); next.run(out) } } The app builds one per header the configuration lists. Macros Manual examples/publish_dyn_stack.rs #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn issue_receipt(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id } } /// The chain comes from configuration: one `Stamp` per header the operator listed. fn app(headers: &[(&str, &str)]) -> impl App { let chain = headers .iter() .map(|(name, value)| -> Arc<dyn PublishDynLayer> { Arc::new(Stamp { name: Str::from((*name).to_owned()), value: Bytes::from((*value).to_owned()), }) }); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .publish_layer(PublishDynStack::new(chain)) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(issue_receipt)) } examples/manual/publish_dyn_stack.rs struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } /// The chain comes from configuration: one `Stamp` per header the operator listed. fn app(headers: &[(&str, &str)]) -> impl App { let chain = headers .iter() .map(|(name, value)| -> Arc<dyn PublishDynLayer> { Arc::new(Stamp { name: Str::from((*name).to_owned()), value: Bytes::from((*value).to_owned()), }) }); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .publish_layer(PublishDynStack::new(chain)) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", IssueReceipt).reply().build()) }) }

A publish layer wraps every message the app's handlers publish: it changes the message, observes the send, or refuses it. A PublishLayer gets the Outgoing message and a PublishNext. next.run(out) runs the layers after it and then the broker send. Before that call the layer may change the message, its headers for one; after it, the layer sees the send's result. An error returned without the call refuses the publish. RustStream::publish_layer adds a layer to the app, before the first with_broker; the layer is Clone. It wraps a reply and every message sent through an Out slot. A message passes its position's transforms first, then the app's publish layers, then the send. The last publish layer added runs outermost, the reverse of the order of handler layers. A handler mounted through a router is the exception on the slot side: its slots take their own transforms, not the app's publish layers; its replies pass through them. The chain is one type, with no dynamic call. A layer has no macro form: the same impl serves both forms, and only the handler differs. A chain chosen when the app starts goes into a PublishDynStack.

The layer names the service on every message it publishes. examples/publish_layer.rs /// Names the service on every message it publishes. #[derive(Clone)] struct Origin { service: &'static str, } impl PublishLayer for Origin { async fn on_publish<'a, N: PublishPipeline, P: Publisher>( &'a self, out: &'a mut Outgoing<'a>, next: PublishNext<'a, N, P>, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { out.headers_mut().insert("origin", self.service); next.run(out).await } } Macros Manual examples/publish_layer.rs #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn issue_receipt(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) // The replies and the `Out` slot publishes of the handlers below pass through it. .publish_layer(Origin { service: "billing" }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(issue_receipt)) } examples/manual/publish_layer.rs struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) // The replies and the `Out` slot publishes of the handlers below pass through it. .publish_layer(Origin { service: "billing" }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", IssueReceipt).reply().build()) }) }

Settings the attribute leaves open are chained where the handler is mounted: name, workers, failure policy, batch size and start position. Each setting has two spellings: a clause in the attribute, or a method of SubscriberSettings at the mount site. At the mount site In the attribute What it sets .name(name) #[subscriber("name")] the subscription a source left open .workers(n), .workers_by_key(n) workers(n), workers(n, by_key) how many deliveries run at once (workers) .threads(n), .threads_by_key(n) threads(n), threads(n, by_key) dedicated threads for a handler that computes (threads) .on_failure(policies) on_failure(panic = .., decode = ..) what a panic or an undecodable payload does (failures) .batch(n) none the batch size of a &[T] handler (batches) .start_at(position) start_at(position) where a replayable subscription opens (start_at) A setting the attribute named is fixed in the definition's type, so naming it again at the mount site does not compile. The mount site is where a value known only at run time goes: a name from configuration, a pool size per deployment. Counts are NonZeroUsize, and the nonzero! macro writes one: nonzero!(4) compiles and nonzero!(0) does not. on_failure takes a FailurePolicies value: one FailurePolicy for a panic and one for a decode failure. A subscription takes workers or threads, not both: they fill one position. batch exists only on a batch handler, and a batch handler does not mount without it. start_at compiles only against a broker whose subscriptions are replayable. A broker crate adds steps of its own to the same chain, such as a consumer group, in the broker's vocabulary. In the manual form the same methods chain on subscriber(source, body) before .build().

Macros Manual examples/subscriber_settings.rs /// Everything is left to the mount site: the name, the pool, the failure policy. #[subscriber] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( bill.name("orders") .workers(nonzero!(4)) // A payload that does not decode is acked and skipped, not dropped. .on_failure(FailurePolicies::default().with_decode(FailurePolicy::Skip)), ) }) } examples/manual/subscriber_settings.rs struct Bill; impl Handle<Order> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<Name>::new(), Bill) .name("orders") .workers(nonzero!(4)) // A payload that does not decode is acked and skipped, not dropped. .on_failure(FailurePolicies::default().with_decode(FailurePolicy::Skip)) .build(), ) }) }

How a handler answers a message and publishes to other destinations. A handler publishes in two ways. Returning a value is a reply, the default when the handler answers on one destination. Taking a publisher as an Out slot is for a destination chosen at run time, or several at once, another broker's included. Either way the handler never holds a publisher that is not connected: the mount site names a publish policy, and startup pairs it with the connected broker. A message type declares its own destination, and one builder publishes every message.

A handler consumes from one broker and publishes through another, named by a token the target broker mints before registration. bindable() wraps the target broker in a Bindable. bind(policy) mints a Bound token, before any scope is built. The token is a publish policy: it goes where a policy goes, .out_reply(token) for a reply and .out(marker, token) for a slot. The wrapper is what with_broker registers for the target, and startup pairs the token with that broker once it connects. The example labels its two scopes with with_broker_labeled, so a test tells them apart with broker_named. A task beside the service gets a live publisher from a token with RunningApp::publisher, as on the HTTP page.

Macros Manual examples/cross_broker.rs fn app() -> impl App { // The target broker is wrapped first, so its token exists before either scope is built. let west = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); let to_west = west.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("bridge", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled("east", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // Consumed in the east, answered in the west. b.include(mirror).out_reply(to_west) }) .with_broker_labeled("west", west, |b| b.include(record)) } examples/manual/cross_broker.rs fn app() -> impl App { // The target broker is wrapped first, so its token exists before either scope is built. let west = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); let to_west = west.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("bridge", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled("east", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // Consumed in the east, answered in the west. b.include(subscriber("orders", Mirror).reply().build()) .out_reply(to_west) }) .with_broker_labeled("west", west, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders.mirrored", Record).build()) }) }

An Out slot hands a handler a live publisher as a parameter: one marker per slot, bound to a publish policy at the mount site. A slot is for a destination chosen at run time, or for several destinations at once, another broker's included. Out(out): Out<impl Publisher> names a capability, never a broker's publisher type, so the same handler mounts on a production broker and on its in-process test transport. The capability is Publisher, or a narrower one: TransactionalPublisher, OwnedTransactions or RequestReply. A single unnamed slot is DefaultSlot. A handler with several slots names a marker per parameter: a unit struct that derives OutSlot. Its #[publishes(..)] list is what may leave through the slot, and what the generated AsyncAPI document reports for it. An optional third position, Out<impl Publisher, Marker, (A, B)>, narrows what this handler publishes through the slot. The mount site binds each marker with .out(marker, policy), in any order, and the chain goes on to the next include. A transform written after an .out(..) belongs to that slot. A slot that is never bound, a marker the handler does not declare, and a publish of a type outside the list do not compile. A body publishes through the slot with the publish builder. A slot may also take a reply: one handler returns its answer and publishes through slots beside it. The runtime's own retry copies leave through one more slot, Retry.

One unnamed slot. Macros Manual examples/out_slots.rs /// One unnamed slot: the publisher arrives live, and `Event` leaves the destination to the call. #[subscriber("ingress")] async fn forward(event: &Event, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { if out.message(event).to("egress").publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/out_slots.rs /// One unnamed slot: the entry arrives live, and `Event` leaves the destination to the call. struct Forward; impl<Egress> Handle<Event, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Forward where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, event: &Event, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(event) .to("egress") .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Two named slots, each with what it may publish. Macros Manual examples/out_slots.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders.confirmed")] struct Confirmed { id: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Audit { id: u64, } /// A slot marker lists what may leave through the slot. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Confirmed)] struct Orders; #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Audit)] struct Trail; #[subscriber("orders.incoming")] async fn confirm( event: &Event, Out(orders): Out<impl Publisher, Orders>, Out(trail): Out<impl Publisher, Trail>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if orders .message(&Confirmed { id: event.id }) .publish() .await .is_err() || trail .message(&Audit { id: event.id }) .to("audit") .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/out_slots.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Confirmed { id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Confirmed { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders.confirmed"; } impl MessageHeaders for Confirmed { type Contract = NoHeaders; } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Audit { id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Audit { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Audit { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// A slot marker lists what may leave through the slot. struct Orders; impl OutSlot for Orders { const NAME: &'static str = "Orders"; // `Confirmed` fixes its destination, so no transform on this slot may name one. type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Orders> for Confirmed {} struct Trail; impl OutSlot for Trail { const NAME: &'static str = "Trail"; // `Audit` leaves its destination open, so a transform on this slot may name it. type Destination = Names; } impl PublishedThrough<Trail> for Audit {} struct Confirm; impl<O, T> Handle<Event, (), Outs<(O, T)>> for Confirm where O: OutEntry<Orders, Wire: Publisher>, T: OutEntry<Trail, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, event: &Event, outs: &Outs<(O, T)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if outs .get(Orders) .message(&Confirmed { id: event.id }) .publish() .await .is_err() || outs .get(Trail) .message(&Audit { id: event.id }) .to("audit") .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/out_slots.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(forward) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) // Each marker binds its own policy, in any order. .include(confirm) .out(Orders, Publish) .out(Trail, Publish) }) } examples/manual/out_slots.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("ingress", Forward).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) // Each marker binds its own policy, in any order. .include(subscriber("orders.incoming", Confirm).build()) .out(Orders, Publish) .out(Trail, Publish) }) }

A message type declares where it goes: a fixed name, a name template with a setter per placeholder, or no name, left to the call. #[derive(Outgoing)] makes a type publishable, and #[outgoing(name = "..")] declares its destination. A fixed name, "orders.confirmed", resolves the destination for every call site, so the publish needs no .to(..). A name template, "orders.{tenant}.placed", opens .to() with one setter per placeholder, and the publish exists only once every placeholder is bound. A template renders its name on each publish; a fixed name costs nothing per publish. A type without a name takes .to("dest") at every call site. A reply type declares a fixed name or none: the runtime publishes the reply and has nothing to bind a template's placeholders with, so a reply to a template does not compile. The generated AsyncAPI document reports each declared destination, a template as a channel with parameters. Without the macros, the type implements OutgoingDestination by hand: FixedName, NameTemplate or CallerName as its Form. A template there also names the builder of its setters through TemplateAddress. The same attribute declares the message's header contract, #[outgoing(headers = Meta)], described on the Outgoing page of typed headers.

The three forms of a destination. Macros Manual examples/destinations.rs /// A fixed name: every publish of this type goes to `orders.confirmed`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders.confirmed")] struct OrderConfirmed { id: u64, } /// A name template: each placeholder becomes a setter on the publish builder. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders.{tenant}.placed")] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, } /// No name: the call site names the destination. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Notice { id: u64, } examples/manual/destinations.rs /// A fixed name: every publish of this type goes to `orders.confirmed`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct OrderConfirmed { id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for OrderConfirmed { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders.confirmed"; } impl MessageHeaders for OrderConfirmed { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// A name template: the type names the builder that carries one setter per placeholder. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for OrderPlaced { type Form = NameTemplate; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders.{tenant}.placed"; const PARAMETERS: &'static [&'static str] = &["tenant"]; } impl MessageHeaders for OrderPlaced { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl<Cont> TemplateAddress<Cont> for OrderPlaced { type Builder = PlacedAt<Cont, MissingSegment<Tenant>>; fn begin(cont: Cont) -> Self::Builder { PlacedAt { cont, tenant: MissingSegment::new(), } } } /// No name: the call site names the destination. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Notice { id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Notice { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Notice { type Contract = NoHeaders; } Each publish fills only what its type leaves open. Macros Manual examples/destinations.rs #[subscriber("orders.incoming")] async fn route(order: &Order, Out(orders): Out<impl Publisher, Orders>) -> HandlerOutcome { let confirmed = orders .message(&OrderConfirmed { id: order.id }) .publish() .await; let placed = orders .message(&OrderPlaced { id: order.id }) .to() .tenant(&order.tenant) .publish() .await; let notice = orders .message(&Notice { id: order.id }) .to("notices") .publish() .await; if confirmed.is_err() || placed.is_err() || notice.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/destinations.rs struct Route; impl<O> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(O,)>> for Route where O: OutEntry<Orders, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(O,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let orders = outs.get(Orders); let confirmed = orders .message(&OrderConfirmed { id: order.id }) .publish() .await; let placed = orders .message(&OrderPlaced { id: order.id }) .to() .tenant(&order.tenant) .publish() .await; let notice = orders .message(&Notice { id: order.id }) .to("notices") .publish() .await; if confirmed.is_err() || placed.is_err() || notice.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

One builder publishes every message: message(&value), the positions its type leaves open, then publish(). A slot, a transaction and any bare Publisher start a publish with message(&value) and return a PublishBuilder. The positions the message type leaves open come next. .to(name) names the destination of a type that declares none, and a template opens .to() with its setters, as on the Destinations page. A publish whose destination is still open does not compile. .with_headers(..) takes the type's declared header contract by reference, or a HeaderMap built by hand. The headers on the wire are the publisher's base headers with the call site's over them, key by key. .with_codec(codec) names a codec for this one publish, over the slot's and the app's. A Serialized value carries its own bytes and has no codec position. A broker adds steps of its own for its per-message settings. publish() encodes the value and sends it, and returns PublishError on failure. Encode and Serialize mean the value did not encode, and a retry of the same value fails the same way. Publish carries the broker's own error. On a slot the message passes the slot's transforms before the send, and the app's publish layers where they apply.

Macros Manual examples/publish_builder.rs #[subscriber("shipments")] async fn notify(shipment: &Shipment, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("carrier", shipment.carrier.clone()); let sent = out .message(&Notice { id: shipment.id }) .to(format!("notices.{}", shipment.region)) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // A value that does not encode fails the same way on every attempt. Err(PublishError::Encode(_) | PublishError::Serialize(_)) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/publish_builder.rs struct Notify; impl<Egress> Handle<Shipment, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Notify where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("carrier", shipment.carrier.clone()); let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&Notice { id: shipment.id }) .to(format!("notices.{}", shipment.region)) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // A value that does not encode fails the same way on every attempt. Err(PublishError::Encode(_) | PublishError::Serialize(_)) => { Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } Err(_) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), } } }

A broker's per-message settings, such as a priority, a QoS or a key: defaulted by the publish policy, set per publish by the broker's own steps. A broker declares its settings as Publisher::Options, a type of its own with every field optional. The publish policy at the mount site holds the defaults. A body that sets one bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = ..>, _> and imports the broker's prelude, whose extension trait adds the steps to the builder. A step sets one field for one publish; a field no step touches keeps the policy's default. A reply and a retry copy have no call site, so a transform that writes the broker's options sets them there. A transform runs after the call site, so it wins a field both of them set. A setting reaches the broker's publisher as a value, not as a header, and a test reads it back with with_options. The memory broker's publisher has no settings, so the example wraps it with a priority the way a networked broker ships one, and turns the priority into a header the test can read. A service on a networked broker imports the broker's own options and steps instead.

The body sets the priority of an express order; the mount site sets the default. Macros Manual examples/per_message_options.rs /// The bound names the broker's settings, so the broker's own steps appear on the builder. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn ship( order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher<Options = PriorityOptions>, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = out.message(order).to("shipments"); let sent = if order.express { shipment.priority(9).publish().await } else { shipment.publish().await }; if sent.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/per_message_options.rs /// The bound names the broker's settings, so the broker's own steps appear on the builder. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher<Options = PriorityOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = outs.get(Shipments).message(order).to("shipments"); let sent = if order.express { shipment.priority(9).publish().await } else { shipment.publish().await }; if sent.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } A reply takes its settings from a transform. Macros Manual examples/per_message_options.rs /// A reply has no call site, so a transform sets its settings. struct LowPriority; impl<K: ContextKind> PublishTransform<K, PriorityOptions> for LowPriority { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PriorityOptions>, _cx: &K::View<'_>, ) { options .get_or_insert_with(PriorityOptions::default) .priority = Some(1); } } #[subscriber("receipt-requests", reply)] async fn issue_receipt(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id } } examples/manual/per_message_options.rs /// A reply has no call site, so a transform sets its settings. struct LowPriority; impl<K: ContextKind> PublishTransform<K, PriorityOptions> for LowPriority { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PriorityOptions>, _cx: &K::View<'_>, ) { options .get_or_insert_with(PriorityOptions::default) .priority = Some(1); } } struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } Macros Manual examples/per_message_options.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The policy holds the defaults: priority 3 unless a step says otherwise. b.include(ship) .out(Shipments, PriorityPublish::default().priority(3)) .include(issue_receipt) .out_reply(PriorityPublish::default().priority(3)) .transform(LowPriority) }) } examples/manual/per_message_options.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The policy holds the defaults: priority 3 unless a step says otherwise. b.include(subscriber("orders", Ship).build()) .out(Shipments, PriorityPublish::default().priority(3)) .include(subscriber("receipt-requests", IssueReceipt).reply().build()) .out_reply(PriorityPublish::default().priority(3)) .transform(LowPriority) }) }

The publisher capabilities a broker offers, one trait each, starting with Publisher. A handler names the capability its slot needs, never the broker's publisher type. A slot bound to a policy whose live publisher lacks that capability does not compile. A broker offers only the capabilities its transport has: Kafka-like brokers carry one transaction per producer, and request and reply need a broker that correlates answers.

OwnedTransactions opens independent transactions that own their buffers, so a handler keeps several open on one slot at once. A broker whose transactions are client buffers flushed at commit offers this kind: an AMQP confirms buffer, a Redis pipeline, the memory broker. A handler bounds its slot Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Marker> and calls transaction(). Each call returns a TypedTransaction of its own, and settling one never touches another. Publishes go through the transaction's builder and stay in its buffer until commit() flushes them together. commit() and abort() consume the value, so a publish after settling does not compile. A transaction dropped unsettled discards its buffer, the way an abort does, and logs a warning. The transaction sends from its own buffer: the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers do not run on its messages, and a test reads them on the destination record, published, rather than the slot's. Kafka-like brokers offer only the borrowed kind, TransactionalPublisher.

A transfer books its entries in one transaction and its audit record in another, so an empty transfer keeps the audit record and books nothing. Macros Manual examples/owned_transactions.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Debit, Credit, Audited)] struct Ledger; /// The audit record and the entries settle apart: two transactions open on one slot. #[subscriber("transfers")] async fn book( transfer: &Transfer, Out(ledger): Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(mut audit) = ledger.transaction().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let Ok(mut entries) = ledger.transaction().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let id = transfer.id; if audit.message(&Audited { id }).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } if transfer.amount == 0 { // Nothing to book: the entries go, the audit record stays. if entries.abort().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let amount = transfer.amount; let debit = entries.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = entries.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() || entries.commit().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/owned_transactions.rs struct Ledger; impl OutSlot for Ledger { const NAME: &'static str = "Ledger"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Debit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Credit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Audited {} /// The audit record and the entries settle apart: two transactions open on one slot. struct Book; impl<L> Handle<Transfer, (), Outs<(L,)>> for Book where L: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: OwnedTransactions>, { async fn handle( &self, transfer: &Transfer, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let ledger = outs.get(Ledger); let Ok(mut audit) = ledger.transaction().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let Ok(mut entries) = ledger.transaction().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let id = transfer.id; if audit.message(&Audited { id }).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } if transfer.amount == 0 { // Nothing to book: the entries go, the audit record stays. if entries.abort().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } return Ok(()); } let amount = transfer.amount; let debit = entries.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = entries.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() || entries.commit().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/owned_transactions.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(book).out(Ledger, Publish) }) } examples/manual/owned_transactions.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("transfers", Book).build()) .out(Ledger, Publish) }) }

Publisher is the capability every slot names; a publish policy at the mount site becomes one when startup pairs it with the connected broker. A handler bounds its slot on the capability, Out<impl Publisher>, and never on a broker's publisher type. The same handler then mounts on a production broker and on its in-process test transport unchanged. A policy holds no connection, so it is built anywhere: a broker's prelude names its plain one Publish. Startup pairs each policy with the connected broker, so a handler never holds a publisher that is not connected. A reply with no policy named leaves through the broker's default one, DefaultPublish. A startup hook such as after_startup takes a policy and gets its live publisher, for a publish outside any handler. A bare publisher starts a publish with the same builder, under the default codec. A publisher declares three types. Payload says how its client takes the bytes: Lend when it only reads them, so the runtime lends one reused buffer, and Take when it keeps them. Options are its per-message settings, and Error is what a failed publish returns. Its base_headers go on every message it sends, under the headers of the call site. The narrower capabilities extend it: TransactionalPublisher, OwnedTransactions and RequestReply.

The handler names the capability; the mount site and the startup hook name the policy. Macros Manual examples/publisher.rs /// The bound names a capability, never the broker's publisher type. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn archive(order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { if out .message(order) .to("orders.archive") .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/publisher.rs /// The bound names a capability, never the broker's publisher type. struct Archive; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Archive where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(order) .to("orders.archive") .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/publisher.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A startup hook gets the live publisher of the policy it names. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Started { service: "archive".into(), }) .publish() .await }) // A policy holds no connection; startup pairs it with the connected broker. .include(archive) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) }) } examples/manual/publisher.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A startup hook gets the live publisher of the policy it names. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Started { service: "archive".into(), }) .publish() .await }) // A policy holds no connection; startup pairs it with the connected broker. .include(subscriber("orders", Archive).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) }) }

RequestReply sends a request from a handler and awaits the correlated answer, on a broker that correlates replies natively. NATS-style brokers correlate replies, and the memory broker does too; Kafka and classic queues do not offer this capability. A handler bounds its slot Out<impl RequestReply, Marker>, and the mount site binds the broker's request policy, which its prelude names Request. request(message, timeout) publishes the message and resolves on the first answer, or fails once the time runs out. The request is an OutgoingMessage of bytes the handler encoded, and the answer is the broker's incoming message, which the handler decodes. The request goes to the broker directly, past the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers. The broker names an inbox for the answer: the memory broker puts it in the reply-to header. The responder is an ordinary reply handler whose reply goes to that inbox, through a naming transform. The slot also publishes with the builder, what its #[publishes(..)] list admits.

The handler asks the quote service for a price, then publishes the priced order through the same slot. Macros Manual examples/requester.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Priced)] struct Pricing; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn price(order: &Order, Out(pricing): Out) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(ask) = serde_json::to_vec(&Ask { id: order.id }) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("quotes.ask", ask.as_slice()); let Ok(answer) = pricing.request(request, Duration::from_secs(2)).await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let Ok(quote) = serde_json::from_slice::(answer.payload()) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let priced = Priced { id: order.id, price: quote.price, }; if pricing.message(&priced).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/requester.rs struct Pricing; impl OutSlot for Pricing { const NAME: &'static str = "Pricing"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough for Priced {} struct Price; impl

Handle> for Price where P: OutEntry, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(P,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pricing = outs.get(Pricing); let ask = serde_json::to_vec(&Ask { id: order.id }).map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop())?; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("quotes.ask", ask.as_slice()); let answer = pricing .request(request, Duration::from_secs(2)) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; let quote = serde_json::from_slice::(answer.payload()) .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop())?; let priced = Priced { id: order.id, price: quote.price, }; pricing .message(&priced) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } The responder answers on the inbox the request named. Macros Manual examples/requester.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's request policy: its live publisher correlates replies. b.include(price) .out(Pricing, Request) .include(quote_price) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ToInbox) }) } examples/manual/requester.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's request policy: its live publisher correlates replies. b.include(subscriber("orders", Price).build()) .out(Pricing, Request) .include( subscriber("quotes.ask", QuoteAsk) .reply() .to("quotes.answers") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ToInbox) }) }

TransactionalPublisher puts several publishes in one broker transaction: every reply of a batch, or a scope a handler opens on its slot. Messages published inside a transaction become visible together on commit, or not at all. A batch handler whose reply chain ends with .transactional() publishes every reply of the batch in one transaction, and acks the batch after the commit. A policy whose live publisher has no transactions does not compile there. A broker's prelude names its transactional policy TransactionalPublish. By hand, a handler bounds its slot Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Marker> and calls begin(). It returns a TransactionScope that owns the transaction, and publishes go through the scope's builder. commit() and abort() consume the scope, so a second commit or a publish after settling does not compile. A scope dropped unsettled logs a warning and leaves the broker transaction open, so a handler settles every scope it opens. The scope sends straight into the transaction: the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers do not run on its messages. This is the borrowed kind of transaction: the publisher carries one broker transaction, and one scope is open on it at a time. Kafka-like brokers, whose client holds one transaction per producer, offer this kind only. Brokers whose transactions are client buffers also offer OwnedTransactions.

Every confirmation of a batch in one transaction. Macros Manual examples/transactional_publisher.rs /// Every confirmation of a batch becomes visible at once, on commit. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn confirm(orders: &[Order]) -> Vec<Confirmed> { orders .iter() .map(|order| Confirmed { id: order.id }) .collect() } examples/manual/transactional_publisher.rs /// Every confirmation of a batch becomes visible at once, on commit. struct Confirm; impl Handle<[Order], Vec<Confirmed>> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<Confirmed>, Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Ok(orders .iter() .map(|order| Confirmed { id: order.id }) .collect())) } } A scope opened on a slot: both entries of a payment, or neither. Macros Manual examples/transactional_publisher.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Debit, Credit)] struct Ledger; /// Both entries of a payment, or neither. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn book( payment: &Payment, Out(ledger): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(scope) = ledger.begin().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let (id, amount) = (payment.id, payment.amount); let debit = scope.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = scope.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() { if let Err(err) = scope.abort().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "payments: aborting the ledger transaction failed"); } return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } match scope.commit().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/transactional_publisher.rs struct Ledger; impl OutSlot for Ledger { const NAME: &'static str = "Ledger"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Debit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Credit {} /// Both entries of a payment, or neither. struct Book; impl<L> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(L,)>> for Book where L: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ok(scope) = outs.get(Ledger).begin().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry());
